tagline: Social Security does not ask whether you are sick. It asks whether you can do any job that exists in significant numbers in the national economy. For a Dearborn claimant who worked the Rouge, a kitchen on Warren, or a career overseas, answering that question correctly is what wins the claim.

c.v: About two out of three first applications for Social Security Disability are denied, and most of the people denied are in fact disabled. They are denied because the application did not answer the question Social Security actually asks: not “are you sick?” but “can you do any job that exists in significant numbers in the national economy, given your age, education, and work history?” In Dearborn that question has particular answers. Many claimants spent decades in physical work at the Rouge, the steel works, or the restaurants and groceries on Michigan Avenue and Warren. Many have work history from before they came to the United States. Many will testify through an interpreter. Each of those facts changes how the claim is built.

c.v: Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI)

is for people who worked and paid Social Security taxes: generally 40 work credits, 20 of them in the ten years before disability, fewer for younger workers. The benefit is based on your U.S. earnings record, with Medicare after 24 months of entitlement. A Dearborn autoworker or tradesperson who stopped working in their fifties is a typical SSDI claimant.
Supplemental Security Income (SSI)

is for people with little income and few assets, whether or not they worked: $994 a month for an individual in 2026, reduced by other income, with a $2,000 asset limit (home and one vehicle excluded) and Michigan Medicaid. Many claimants qualify for both, and the applications are filed together. See our
SSDI page

SSI page
Work history abroad and citizenship.

Work performed outside the United States generally does not earn U.S. work credits for SSDI; the U.S. has totalization agreements that count foreign credits with only a limited list of countries. Work history abroad still matters to the disability decision: Social Security considers the skills and exertion of past work wherever it was done. SSI eligibility for noncitizens is limited to certain categories under federal law. Where either issue applies, it is the first question we answer, before the application is filed.

sections.heading: The five-step test, as it is applied to a Dearborn claim

c.v: Social Security uses a five-step sequential evaluation (20 CFR 404.1520), deciding the claim at the first step where the answer is clear.
Are you working above the substantial gainful activity level?

items.v: Earning more than $1,690 a month in 2026 ends the claim at step one.

c.v: Is your impairment severe and expected to last 12 months or result in death?

items.v: A diagnosis is not enough; the record must show functional limits.

Can you do your past relevant work?

items.v: Social Security assesses your residual functional capacity and compares it to the jobs you held in the past five years, including jobs held abroad.

c.v: Can you do any other work?

items.v: Using your RFC, age, education, and work experience under the Medical-Vocational Guidelines (the “grids”). A 55-year-old former line worker limited to sedentary work is generally found disabled under the grids; a 45-year-old with the same limits generally is not.

c.v: grid summary
Language and education.

Since April 2020, Social Security no longer treats inability to communicate in English as a separate education category at step five; education is evaluated by the claimant’s formal schooling and abilities, wherever obtained.
85 Fed. Reg. 10586 and current application

For a Dearborn claimant who does not speak English well, that change makes the medical and vocational evidence carry more of the claim, and makes it more important that the record describes the claimant’s actual limitations accurately.

Social Security provides a free interpreter at every stage, at the field office, by phone, at the consultative examination, and at the hearing; you do not need to bring a family member to interpret, and in most cases should not.

Tell Social Security in writing which language you need. At the hearing, the judge, the vocational expert, and your lawyer speak through the interpreter, and what you say about your limitations is the evidence. We prepare you for that hearing in your language.

Missing a 60-day deadline usually means starting over with a new application. Appeal; do not reapply.

SSDI benefits begin five full months after the established onset date; SSI is not paid for months before the application. Back pay reaches to the onset date (SSDI up to 12 months before the application), and the onset date your lawyer proves sets the amount. The fee is set by federal law: 25 percent of back benefits, capped at the current limit, and nothing if the claim is not approved (42 USC 406(a)). Social Security pays it directly from back pay; ongoing monthly benefits are not subject to it.

faqs.question: Can I have an interpreter at my Social Security hearing?

answer.v: Yes. Social Security provides one free of charge at every stage. Request it in writing and say which language you need. You do not need to bring a family member.

faqs.question: I worked for years before I came to the United States. Does that count?

answer.v: For SSDI work credits, generally not, except under a totalization agreement with a limited list of countries. For the disability decision, yes: Social Security considers what your past work required, wherever it was done.

faqs.question: I don’t speak English well. Does that help my claim?

answer.v: Not by itself since 2020; Social Security no longer treats it as a separate education category. Your claim rests on your medical limitations, your age, your schooling, and your past work.

faqs.question: How long do I have to appeal?

answer.v: Sixty days from the date on the denial notice, plus five days for mailing, at every stage.
At the Detroit or Livonia hearing office, or by video or phone. You can request to appear in person.

faqs.question: I was hurt at the Rouge and get workers’ comp. Can I also get SSDI?

answer.v: Yes, if you meet Social Security’s definition of disability, but the two benefits offset so that the combined amount does not exceed a federal limit. We coordinate both.

faqs.question: What does a Dearborn disability lawyer cost?

answer.v: Twenty-five percent of your back benefits, capped by federal law, paid by Social Security from the back pay. Nothing if you do not win.
